title: MOBI: Monolithic Graph-Language Modeling Beyond Modality Interference

problem.claim: Graph-Language Models aim to provide structure-grounded reasoning, but graph and language modalities can interfere with one another.

gap.claim: Modular approaches with separate graph encoders have limited cross-modal interaction and do not adequately resolve modality interference.

contributions.claim: MOBI is a monolithic graph-language model that unifies graph encoding and language decoding in a single backbone for end-to-end graph-text fusion.

MOBI combines a dual-pathway transformer, progressive interaction scheduling, and correlation-guided attribute perturbation to preserve linguistic knowledge, regulate cross-modal information flow, and discourage textual shortcuts.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report extensive experiments on 11 datasets across various settings.
The authors report that MOBI consistently outperforms modular baselines.

narrative_sequence.summary: Graph-Language Models seek structure-grounded reasoning but face interference between structural and linguistic information.
Modular models separate graph encoding from language decoding to mitigate interference.
This separation limits cross-modal interaction while leaving modality interference unresolved.
MOBI unifies graph encoding and language decoding in one backbone and uses three mechanisms to manage interference.
Experiments on 11 datasets reportedly show consistent improvement over modular baselines.

source_observation.claim: Separating graph encoding from language decoding can reduce cross-modal interaction while not fully resolving interference.

interpretation.claim: Modality separation may trade off interference control against effective information fusion.

application.claim: When integrating heterogeneous modalities, consider unified representations with explicit information-flow controls.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this design generalizes beyond the reported graph-language settings.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the 11 datasets, evaluation metrics, baseline configurations, or quantitative improvements.
The abstract does not provide ablations isolating the effects of the three proposed mechanisms.
The abstract does not report computational costs, limitations, or reproducibility details.
